discovery: Optical lattice atomic clocks reaching 10^-18 precision

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision measurement
motivation: Katori conceived the optical lattice clock, trapping neutral atoms at a 'magic' wavelength so the lattice light leaves the clock transition unshifted. This combines the Lamb-Dicke confinement of ion clocks with the statistical power of thousands of atoms. Ye turned the idea into metrology-grade instruments. He used ultrastable lasers, frequency combs and control of many-body interactions, including spin-locked degenerate Fermi gases, to reach fractional uncertainties and stabilities near 10^-18 and beyond. Katori's transportable clocks and Ye's millimetre-scale resolution of gravitational redshift within a single atomic sample have turned timekeeping into a sensor for relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental-constant variation and searches for dark matter. These clocks are now driving the redefinition of the SI second. It is a rare case where a conceptually new idea became shared infrastructure that changes what physics can measure.
